displayQuote: We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence is not an act, but a habit

meta.title: Who really said "We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence is not an act, but a habit"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: It's credited to Aristotle everywhere — but the sentence was written by historian Will Durant in The Story of Philosophy (1926), summarizing Aristotle.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence is not an act, but a habit'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Aristotle. Will Durant wrote it in 1926, paraphrasing Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics. Quotle.info traces the source and the misattribution.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This line really is Durant’s. It appears in his 1926 bestseller The Story of Philosophy, where he is summarizing Aristotle’s ethics—so the crediting to Durant is correct, even though the internet overwhelmingly pins it on Aristotle. Durant’s printed sentence reads “we are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act but a habit”; the viral form simply drops the word “then.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Story of Philosophy: The Lives and Opinions of the Greater Philosophers
1926 (Simon & Schuster) · ch. on Aristotle, “Ethics and the Nature of Happiness”
Durant’s own summary of Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics (Bk. II.4, Bk. I.7)

source.excerpt: Excellence is an art won by training and habituation: we do not act rightly because we have virtue or excellence, but we rather have these because we have acted rightly; ‘these virtues are formed in man by his doing the actions’; we are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act but a habit.
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced Will Durant page prints the full passage and attributes it to The Story of Philosophy (1926), footnoting the Aristotle sources Durant is paraphrasing.
WIST files it under Aristotle only to flag that it is “a summary by Will Durant,” not Aristotle’s own words.
A UMass Boston “Quote/Unquote” analysis locates the line on p. 87 of the edition it examined and explains why it keeps getting re-credited to Aristotle.
source.excerptNote: The words in single quotes are Durant quoting Aristotle directly; the rest — including the famous closing sentence — is Durant’s own paraphrase knitting Aristotle’s argument together.

sourceLink.text: Read The Story of Philosophy (Garden City reprint of the 1926 text) at the Internet Archive

source.rightsNote: The Story of Philosophy was first published in 1926, before the 1931 U.S. public-domain cutoff, so the text of that first edition is in the public domain in the United States. (Durant issued a revised edition in 1933; that later revision is a separate copyright, but the sentence appears in the 1926 original.)

author.name: Will Durant
author.heading: Will Durant
author.bio: William James Durant was an American writer and historian who made philosophy and history accessible to a mass audience. His 1926 book The Story of Philosophy was a runaway bestseller and funded the decades of work he and his wife Ariel Durant poured into the eleven-volume The Story of Civilization, for which they won the 1968 Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction. He received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1977.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: This is the internet’s most persistent philosophy misquote: the sentence is almost universally stamped on Aristotle, complete with a toga portrait. Aristotle never wrote it. The wording is Will Durant’s 1926 paraphrase — which is why crediting Durant, as done here, is the accurate call.

items.why: Aristotle never wrote this sentence. Durant composed it while summarizing the Nicomachean Ethics; the underlying idea is Aristotle’s, but the memorable phrasing is Durant’s. WIST and Wikiquote both make this explicit.

items.scope: “Excellence is not an act, but a habit”
items.why: Durant’s printed sentence is “Excellence, then, is not an act but a habit.” The viral form drops “then” and adds a comma — a light clean-up, not a change of meaning.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is Aristotle’s; the sentence is Will Durant’s, from The Story of Philosophy (1926) — as documented on Wikiquote’s sourced Durant page.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: The quote is a near-perfect distillation of Aristotle’s theory of virtue: for Aristotle we become just by doing just acts and brave by doing brave acts — character is built through hexis, settled habit, not through single grand gestures. Durant’s genius was to compress pages of the Nicomachean Ethics into one quotable line.

That compression is exactly why it gets misattributed. Readers assume so clean an encapsulation of Aristotle must be Aristotle — and a Greek philosopher’s name carries more authority on a poster than a 20th-century popularizer’s. The irony is tidy: a sentence about the habits we repeat has itself been repeated into a false attribution.
context.pull: The thought is Aristotle’s. The sentence is Durant’s.
